content: Magnesium hydroxide, when combined with mineral oil, is typically administered at a dose of 45-60 mL per day orally, either as a single dose at bedtime or divided into multiple doses. The liquid form can be taken in doses of 5-15 mL orally as needed, up to every 6 hours. Magnesium hydroxide can interact with various medications by altering their absorption or effectiveness. For example: 1. Baloxavir marboxil: Magnesium hydroxide reduces its absorption in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract due to cation binding. This interaction can significantly lower plasma levels, as shown in animal studies, though human studies are lacking. It is recommended to avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 2. Demeclocycline, doxycycline, minocycline, oxytetracycline, tetracycline, omadacycline, and sarecycline: Magnesium hydroxide decreases their absorption in the GI tract, reducing their effectiveness. This applies only to oral forms of both agents. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative therapy. If unavoidable, separate doses by several hours. 3. Eltrombopag: Magnesium hydroxide significantly reduces its absorption in the GI tract. This interaction is contraindicated, and doses should be separated by at least 4 hours. 4. Infigratinib, pazopanib, ponatinib, and crizotinib: Magnesium hydroxide increases gastric pH, reducing the solubility and bioavailability of these drugs. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative therapy. If unavoidable, administer the drug 2 hours before or after magnesium hydroxide. 5. Ciprofloxacin, gemifloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and ofloxacin: Magnesium hydroxide reduces their bioavailability by up to 90% due to cation binding in the GI tract. Administer these antibiotics at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after magnesium hydroxide. 6. Rifampin, dolutegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir, and raltegravir: Magnesium hydroxide reduces their plasma levels by cation binding in the GI tract. Administer these drugs 2 hours before or 6 hours after magnesium hydroxide. 7. Vitamin D: Co-administration with magnesium hydroxide can increase serum magnesium levels, particularly in patients with renal impairment. Avoid this combination in patients with chronic kidney disease. 8. Mineral oil: This reduces the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) and certain medications like digoxin, beta carotene, and oral contraceptives. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Thiazide and loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, bumetanide): These drugs increase renal clearance of magnesium, potentially lowering magnesium levels. Monitor magnesium levels closely. 10. Amiloride, spironolactone, and triamterene: These potassium-sparing diuretics decrease renal clearance of magnesium, potentially increasing magnesium levels. Monitor for hypermagnesemia. 11. Anticoagulants (e.g., enoxaparin, heparin, dabigatran): Mineral oil reduces their absorption in the GI tract. Monitor closely for reduced anticoagulant effects. 12. Pancrelipase: Magnesium hydroxide may antagonize the effects of pancreatic enzymes. Use caution and monitor for reduced efficacy. 13. Phosphate binders (e.g., sodium or potassium phosphates): Magnesium hydroxide binds dietary phosphate, reducing serum phosphate levels. Use alternatives if available. 14. Amphotericin B and aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin, tobramycin): These drugs increase renal clearance of magnesium, potentially leading to hypomagnesemia. Monitor magnesium levels closely. 15. Estrogens (e.g., estradiol, conjugated estrogens): These may shift magnesium from the blood to tissue storage, reducing serum magnesium levels. Monitor magnesium levels if co-administered. 16. Lanthanum carbonate: Magnesium hydroxide binds to lanthanum in the GI tract, reducing its absorption. Administer lanthanum at least 2 hours before or after magnesium hydroxide. 17. Nitrofurantoin: Magnesium hydroxide reduces its absorption in the GI tract. Use caution and monitor for reduced efficacy. 18. Deflazacort: Co-administration with magnesium hydroxide may exacerbate hypokalemia. Monitor potassium levels closely. 19. Pexidartinib: Magnesium hydroxide reduces its absorption. Separate doses by at least 2 hours. 20. Vismodegib: Drugs that increase gastric pH, such as magnesium hydroxide, may reduce its solubility and bioavailability. Monitor closely for reduced efficacy. In summary, magnesium hydroxide and mineral oil can interact with a wide range of medications, primarily by altering their absorption in the GI tract or affecting serum levels. Careful consideration of timing, dose separation, and alternative therapies is essential to minimize these interactions.
